title: Statements: if and switch
hook: Blocks `{ }` define scope. `if` takes a bool — not a truthy number. Basic `switch` dispatches on a constant; pattern matching is a later module.

sections.heading: Blocks and if/else
sections.prose: A statement block introduces a scope: locals declared inside are not visible outside. `if (condition)` requires a `bool`. There is no `if (retries)` like JavaScript; write `if (retries > 0)`. Braces are optional for a single statement and mandatory in every style guide you should follow — dangling else is real. `else if` chains are just nested else. Use this for auth-provider branching (LTI vs local) when the discriminator is a simple enum or string constant.

snippets.label: if requires bool; basic switch on a token issuer
snippets.explanation: Classic switch needs `break` (or `return`/`throw`/`goto case`) to avoid falling through. `goto case` is the explicit fall-through. Pattern switches come in module 11.

sections.heading: Basic switch only
sections.prose: The statement form `switch (expr) { case 1: ... break; }` compares to constant cases. No `when` clauses, no property patterns here. The switch expression `issuer switch { "lti" => ..., _ => ... }` is still pattern matching — skip it until that module so you do not mix stories in an interview.

interviewTakeaways: `if` conditions are `bool` only; C# will not coerce numbers or strings.
Classic switch is equality to constants plus mandatory break (or jump).
Blocks control definite assignment and lifetime of locals.
commonPitfalls: Writing `if (count)` after years of JS — it does not compile.
Omitting `break` and expecting implicit fall-through like C.
Using a switch expression in an interview while claiming you have not covered patterns yet.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS `if (x)` is truthy. C# `if (x)` needs bool. JS switch falls through by default; C# requires an explicit jump.
